The Collection (for the Saints)
thuh kuh-LEK-shuhn
noun (Pauline doctrine)
From Latin colligere, to gather together; in Paul, the logia or gathering "for the saints" (1 Cor 16:1), a relief offering for the poor believers at Jerusalem.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Collection was Paul's great gathering of relief among the Gentile churches for the poor saints at Jerusalem. He charged the Corinthians, "Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him" (1 Cor 16:2), and he set the churches of Macedonia and Achaia to the same grace. He named its purpose plainly: "it hath pleased them of Macedonia and Achaia to make a certain contribution for the poor saints which are at Jerusalem" (Rom 15:26). He grounded it in a debt of fellowship: the Gentiles, made partakers of the Jews' spiritual things, were bound "to minister unto them in carnal things" (Rom 15:27). In 2 Corinthians 8—9 Paul unfolds the whole grace of giving—the Macedonians' liberality in poverty, the example of Christ who "though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor," and the promise that "God loveth a cheerful giver." Thus the Collection sealed the unity of Jew and Gentile in one body, the wall broken down, fellowship proved by liberality. This dictionary confesses that Christian giving is a grace wrought by God, an act of worship, and a bond of love between the members of Christ's church.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Paul's relief offering gathered among the Gentile churches for the poor saints at Jerusalem; the great New Testament instance of the grace of giving and a seal of Jew-Gentile fellowship.

expand to see more

THE COLLECTION, noun. Paul's gathering of funds among the Gentile churches for the poor saints at Jerusalem.

Ordered on the first day of the week, "as God hath prospered him."

Named in Romans 15:26 as "a certain contribution for the poor saints which are at Jerusalem."

It requires cheerful, proportionate, grace-wrought giving, and it forbids constraint and grudging.

It sealed the fellowship of Jew and Gentile in one body and proved love by liberality.

📖 Key Scripture

1 Cor 16:1 — "Now concerning the collection for the saints, as I have given order to the churches of Galatia, even so do ye."

1 Cor 16:2 — "Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him, that there be no gatherings when I come."

Rom 15:26 — "For it hath pleased them of Macedonia and Achaia to make a certain contribution for the poor saints which are at Jerusalem."

2 Cor 9:7 — "Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the lesson is the recovery of giving as grace and worship rather than as obligation or sentiment.

expand to see more

The Collection is not the subject of modern ideological dispute, yet its doctrine is widely flattened. Some reduce giving to mere fundraising and pressure; others, reacting, treat it as wholly optional and unstructured. Paul holds both error in check: the giving is ordered ("upon the first day of the week"), proportionate ("as God hath prospered him"), and free ("not grudgingly, or of necessity"). It is neither a tax wrung by guilt nor a whim left to mood, but a grace.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the theological weight Paul places on the Collection: it is grounded in the example of Christ, who became poor to make many rich, and it is the proof of fellowship between Jew and Gentile in one body. Giving to the saints is service rendered to Christ Himself and a visible bond of the church's unity. To recover this is to see the offering not as the price of admission to worship but as an act of worship flowing from grace received.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Latin colligere, to gather; in Paul the logia of relief for the Jerusalem poor.

expand to see more

Latin colligere, collectus, to gather together, yields English collection.

Paul's word in 1 Cor 16:1 is logia, a collection or gathering of money.

In 2 Cor 8—9 he calls it charis, grace, and diakonia, ministry.

He names it also koinōnia, the fellowship of the saints in giving.

The terms root Christian liberality in grace received and fellowship expressed.

Usage

"Paul organized the Collection across Galatia, Macedonia, and Achaia for the relief of Jerusalem's poor saints."

"The Collection proved that Gentile believers owed a debt of love to the church that first received the promises."

"In teaching the Collection, Paul set forth the grace of giving and the gladness of the cheerful giver."
